papers.note: The MultiMedQA and Med-PaLM paper, and the origin of the multi axis human evaluation framework used since.
papers.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities, but the bar for clinical applications is high. Attempts to assess the clinical knowledge of models typically rely on automated evaluations based on limited benchmarks. Here, to address these limitations, we present MultiMedQA, a benchmark combining six existing medical question answering datasets spanning professional medicine, research and consumer queries and a new dataset of medical questions searched online, HealthSearchQA. We propose a human evaluation framework for model answers along multiple axes including factuality, comprehension, reasoning, possible harm and bias. In addition, we evaluate Pathways Language Model (PaLM, a 540-billion parameter LLM) and its instruction-tuned variant, Flan-PaLM on MultiMedQA. Using a combination of prompting strategies, Flan-PaLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on every MultiMedQA multiple-choice dataset (MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) clinical topics), including 67.6% accuracy on MedQA (US Medical Licensing Exam-style questions), surpassing the prior state of the art by more than 17%. However, human evaluation reveals key gaps. To resolve this, we introduce instruction prompt tuning, a parameter-efficient approach for aligning LLMs to new domains using a few exemplars. The resulting model, Med-PaLM, performs encouragingly, but remains inferior to clinicians. We show that comprehension, knowledge recall and reasoning improve with model scale and instruction prompt tuning, suggesting the potential utility of LLMs in medicine.
papers.explain_beginner: This is the paper where Google researchers showed that a general-purpose AI model, without any medical schooling, could pass US medical licensing exam questions. That was a jaw-dropping result in 2022 and started the wave of AI-in-medicine products. They also introduced a benchmark called MultiMedQA that the field still uses to test new medical AI systems.
papers.explain_business: This is the moment clinical AI stopped being theoretical. A general-purpose model, not built for medicine, cleared USMLE-style questions and set a new bar overnight. For any organisation running or buying clinical decision-support software, the immediate implication is that base-model gains now translate into clinical-benchmark gains almost directly, and that vendor claims should be validated against a standard set (MultiMedQA) rather than a bespoke internal one that is easy to game.
papers.explain_practitioner: Singhal et al. introduce MultiMedQA (six existing sets plus HealthSearchQA) and show Flan-PaLM 540B reaches 67.6% on MedQA-USMLE with prompt engineering alone, a 17-point jump over the prior state of the art. Instruction prompt tuning yields Med-PaLM, which narrows but does not close the gap to clinicians on a human-evaluated axis set (factuality, reasoning, potential harm, bias). It is the paper that established medical multiple-choice benchmarks as a real evaluation surface and standardised the human-eval axes now used across clinical LLM papers.

papers.note: The primer most clinicians have actually read, which makes it the right shared reference in client conversations.
papers.title: Large language models in medicine
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models, the AI systems behind tools like ChatGPT, are being rapidly adopted in medicine. They show promise in tasks ranging from helping doctors pass licensing exams to automatically summarizing patient records. This survey examines how these models are entering healthcare and what they can do. Understanding these capabilities matters because they could transform how doctors work and improve patient care, but we need reliable information about what they can and cannot do.
papers.explain_business: Large language models are moving into healthcare applications with measurable technical capabilities demonstrated across multiple domains. Organizations considering adoption should recognize that viable use cases exist, from clinical decision support to documentation management. However, the landscape is still rapidly evolving with diverse model types showing different strengths. Decision-makers should treat this as an emerging opportunity requiring careful evaluation of specific applications rather than broad implementation, informed by documented performance on relevant medical tasks.
papers.explain_practitioner: This primer reviews the emerging applications of large language models in clinical practice and medical research. The scope includes systems demonstrating performance on standardized medical assessments and document processing applications. The authors, publishing through KOSMI's special issue, synthesize current developments in LLM deployment across healthcare domains. The key finding is that multiple specialized implementations exist, each with distinct capabilities, requiring practitioners to understand specific use cases and performance characteristics when evaluating integration into clinical workflows.

papers.note: The standard reference on why clinical AI stalls between research and practice, still the clearest statement of the gap.
papers.title: Key challenges for delivering clinical impact with artificial intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers have created many promising artificial intelligence tools for medicine, but few actually make it into hospitals and clinics where patients can benefit from them. This paper explains why that gap exists. The main obstacles include technical challenges with how AI learns from data, practical difficulties in rolling out new systems, and the need for proper testing and regulation. The authors argue that AI healthcare tools must be rigorously tested like new drugs, clearly explained to doctors, and carefully monitored after release to ensure they truly help patients.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations considering AI investments should recognize that research success does not guarantee clinical utility or patient benefit. Successful deployment requires investment in rigorous clinical validation, regulatory navigation, and post-implementation monitoring rather than rapid adoption of promising prototypes. Decision-makers must prioritize vendors demonstrating transparent performance metrics relevant to clinical workflows, clear explainability of algorithmic decisions, and evidence of effectiveness across diverse patient populations. This framework protects organizations from deploying ineffective or biased systems while positioning them to capture genuine competitive advantages from AI innovations.
papers.explain_practitioner: This paper identifies critical barriers preventing clinical deployment of healthcare AI systems. Beyond core machine learning challenges, key obstacles include implementing rigorous randomized controlled trials for validation, developing clinically meaningful performance metrics, and ensuring regulatory frameworks that enable innovation while protecting patients. The authors emphasize the necessity of representative test datasets, mechanisms for comparative evaluation, and mitigation strategies against dataset shift, confounding, and algorithmic bias. Essential improvements require enhancing model interpretability, reducing generalization failures across populations, and measuring outcomes beyond accuracy metrics to include clinical care quality.

papers.note: Balanced account of both democratised access and misinformation risk across practice, research and education.
papers.title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines AI tools called large language models that can read and write text nearly as well as humans. Since ChatGPT became popular in late 2022, these tools have attracted interest in medicine. The researchers found that while these models could help make medical knowledge more accessible and improve healthcare, they also pose serious risks like spreading false information and enabling scientific fraud. The paper balances both the promising opportunities and concerning dangers across medical practice, research, and education.
papers.explain_business: Medical organizations face a strategic decision about large language model adoption. The technology promises improved information accessibility and operational efficiency across clinical, research, and educational functions. However, implementation requires substantial risk mitigation strategies addressing accuracy verification, regulatory compliance, and accountability frameworks. Decision-makers should weigh deployment benefits against liability exposure and reputational risks from potential misinformation spread or research misconduct. A cautious, controlled adoption approach with robust oversight mechanisms is advisable before widespread integration.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic review of large language models across three medical domains: clinical practice, research, and education. LLMs demonstrate human-level performance in text comprehension and generation tasks including question answering, summarization, and translation. The key finding identifies a dual-edged impact: these models offer democratization potential for medical information access and knowledge dissemination, yet simultaneously introduce risks through unaccountable outputs that may propagate inaccurate information and facilitate research integrity violations due to insufficient transparency mechanisms.

papers.note: Written for clinical safety professionals appraising AI, which is exactly the audience for a healthcare AI audit.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence, bias and clinical safety
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines how artificial intelligence systems used in healthcare can develop hidden biases that compromise patient safety. The researchers investigated whether AI tools trained on historical medical data might make unfair or incorrect recommendations for certain groups of patients. Understanding these risks matters because hospitals increasingly rely on AI to help diagnose diseases and guide treatment decisions, so catching bias early prevents harm to vulnerable populations.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations adopting AI tools need formal processes to detect and mitigate algorithmic bias before deployment. This paper provides clinical safety professionals with guidance for auditing AI systems to ensure fair treatment across patient populations and protect against liability. Organizations should implement bias assessment as a standard requirement in their AI procurement and governance processes to maintain safety standards and trust.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of AI bias mechanisms within clinical contexts and their safety implications. They examined how training data characteristics, model development practices, and deployment conditions can introduce or amplify discriminatory patterns in AI decision-making. The study identified that clinical bias emerges through multiple pathways and established a framework for clinical safety professionals to evaluate and audit AI systems for these risks before and during implementation.

papers.note: Restricts to studies reporting actual safety outcomes rather than model accuracy, and finds no standardised benchmark exists.
papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Patient Safety Outcomes: Systematic Literature Review
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers examined studies about how artificial intelligence helps keep patients safe in hospitals and clinics. They found fifty-three studies showing that AI systems can catch medical errors, identify high-risk patients, and prevent medication problems. However, the studies used different methods to measure success, making it hard to compare results. The review shows AI has real promise for patient safety, but hospitals need better ways to test these systems before widely adopting them.
papers.explain_business: AI applications can meaningfully improve patient safety through better error detection and medication management, representing valuable risk mitigation opportunities. However, organizations should recognize that existing published systems lack standardized evaluation metrics, making it difficult to assess which solutions deliver genuine clinical value. Before implementing AI systems, executives should prioritize vendors demonstrating real-world validation data and ensuring solutions have been tested in actual clinical environments rather than relying solely on algorithm accuracy metrics.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review analyzed fifty-three quantitative studies integrating machine learning and natural language processing for patient safety outcomes between 2009 and 2019. Studies focused on three areas: clinical alarms using decision trees, clinical reports using support vector machines, and drug safety using decision trees. Key findings revealed that while AI-enabled decision support systems improved error detection and patient stratification, significant heterogeneity existed in both AI methodology and performance reporting. Critically, no standardized evaluation benchmark was identified, limiting cross-study comparison and clinical validation.

papers.note: Compares open source and proprietary medical models and the metrics used to judge them.
papers.title: Large language models in healthcare and medical domain: A review
papers.explain_beginner: This paper surveys how advanced AI language models are being used in healthcare. These models can read and understand medical questions and information remarkably well. The researchers reviewed what these models can do, from identifying medical terms in documents to answering patient questions, and compared different models available to hospitals and clinics. They also explained the measurements used to determine whether these models work properly and identified obstacles that still need solving before widespread use.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations considering LLM deployment should understand that these systems can meaningfully improve clinical documentation processing and information retrieval. This review enables decision-makers to evaluate available options by comparing proprietary versus open-source models and understanding how to measure their performance. However, organizations should recognize significant limitations and constraints remain. The findings indicate LLMs offer genuine efficiency potential in healthcare operations but require careful assessment of specific use cases and ongoing research before large-scale implementation.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive review examines LLM applications across healthcare tasks including named entity recognition, relation extraction, natural language inference, multimodal analysis, document classification, and question-answering. The authors trace development from traditional pretrained language models through current LLMs, evaluate state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source models, and detail performance metrics for biomedical evaluation. The work synthesizes existing healthcare LLM functionalities, assesses comparative effectiveness across implementations, and identifies technical limitations and implementation challenges requiring further research and development.

papers.note: 89 studies across 29 specialties, with a coded taxonomy separating design limitations from output limitations.
papers.title: Current applications and challenges in large language models for patient care: a systematic review
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers studied how artificial intelligence chatbots like ChatGPT are being used to help patients learn about their health and receive personalized medical information. By reviewing 89 studies across different medical fields, they found these tools are mainly being tested to answer patient questions and summarize medical documents. However, the review identified serious challenges, including that these systems sometimes give wrong or incomplete answers, may not work fairly for all patients, and lack transparency about how they were built. This work matters because it shows both the promise and the real problems we need to solve before these tools can safely help patients.
papers.explain_business: Organizations considering LLM deployment in patient-facing healthcare applications should understand that current systems show promise for answering medical questions and generating patient materials but carry significant risks. The review identifies two critical categories of problems: fundamental limitations in how these systems are built and trained, plus reliability issues in their actual outputs. Before investing in implementation, leaders need assurance that systems have been properly validated for medical accuracy, can explain their reasoning, protect patient safety, and perform equitably across diverse populations. This research provides the baseline evaluation framework needed to assess vendor claims and determine readiness for clinical use.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review analyzed 89 peer-reviewed studies from 2022-2023 examining LLM deployment in patient-facing clinical contexts across 29 specialties. The majority focused on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 for medical question answering, information generation, and documentation support. The authors developed a structured taxonomy of limitations divided into design issues, such as insufficient medical training and poor data transparency, and output issues, including reproducibility failures, inaccuracy, incompleteness, safety concerns, and algorithmic bias. The framework establishes benchmarks for evaluating LLM integration in clinical workflows and highlights areas requiring technical improvement before widespread implementation.

papers.note: 392 studies mapped across eight harm domains, with a judgement on where AI is most likely to reduce harm.
papers.title: The potential of artificial intelligence to improve patient safety: a scoping review
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers reviewed nearly 400 studies to understand how artificial intelligence could make hospitals safer for patients. They examined eight major types of medical errors and injuries, from infections to missed diagnoses. The review found that AI could help predict and prevent many of these problems, especially by using new technologies like wearable devices and sensors to monitor patients. AI seems most promising for catching drug problems, sudden patient decline, and diagnostic mistakes where current methods fall short.
papers.explain_business: This review demonstrates substantial commercial and clinical opportunity in deploying AI for patient safety monitoring across hospitals. Investment should prioritize applications addressing drug safety, patient deterioration detection, and diagnostic support, where AI can meaningfully outperform existing approaches. Implementation requires integrating sensor technologies and monitoring devices with AI analytics platforms. The convergence of clinical need, preventability, and high economic impact of these three harm categories presents the strongest business case for healthcare technology vendors and providers.
papers.explain_practitioner: A scoping review of 392 studies examined AI applications across eight adverse event domains in healthcare. Researchers systematically searched MEDLINE and synthesized literature narratively for each domain, evaluating AI potential based on incidence, cost, and preventability. Novel data sources included vital sign monitors, wearables, pressure sensors, and computer vision. Results indicated AI shows greatest promise in adverse drug events, decompensation, and diagnostic errors, where current prevention strategies are limited and multimodal data integration enables superior predictive accuracy.

papers.note: Consensus recommendations from over 200 stakeholders on validation, certification and national safety reporting.
papers.title: Toward a responsible future: recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support
papers.journal: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
papers.explain_beginner: Doctors increasingly use AI tools to help make medical decisions, but we need safeguards to ensure these tools work fairly and safely. Over 200 experts, including doctors, engineers, and patients, met to identify problems and suggest solutions. They recommended four main steps: building trustworthy systems from the start, testing and certifying AI tools before hospitals use them, creating a national system to report problems when they occur, and training doctors properly. This matters because getting AI right in healthcare can save lives, but getting it wrong could harm patients.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations implementing AI for clinical decisions face regulatory uncertainty and liability risks. This paper provides a roadmap for managing those risks: establish internal validation processes before deployment, maintain continuous monitoring systems to detect problems, and invest in staff training and clear documentation. Organizations that adopt these recommendations early can demonstrate responsible AI governance to regulators and stakeholders, potentially gaining competitive advantage. The recommendations also suggest future national safety reporting standards, which executives should anticipate when planning AI investments in clinical settings.
papers.explain_practitioner: This consensus study brought together 200 stakeholders through webinars and a workshop to develop recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support systems. Through qualitative analysis and iterative consensus-building, the group identified four key areas: designing systems with safety and trustworthiness as core principles, establishing validation and certification protocols before deployment, implementing national-level safety monitoring and adverse event reporting mechanisms, and requiring comprehensive documentation and end-user training. The recommendations address critical gaps in current practices around explainability, fairness, model governance, and regulatory oversight needed for responsible clinical AI integration.

papers.note: 102 studies covering 2.8 million patients, only 45 percent used high evidence validation and only 14 percent shared data.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Surgery: A Systematic Review of Use and Validation
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers reviewed over 100 studies involving millions of patients to understand how artificial intelligence is being used in surgery. They found that AI tools are mainly helping doctors assess risks before operations and make better decisions. However, most AI systems haven't been properly tested to ensure they're safe and accurate. The study created a scoring system to help doctors evaluate whether an AI tool is trustworthy enough to use in real hospitals.
papers.explain_business: This analysis demonstrates AI adoption in surgery remains high-risk due to poor validation standards. Most applications focus on preoperative assessment, representing a moderate market opportunity. The critical bottleneck is that 55% of AI systems lack rigorous validation, creating liability concerns for healthcare organizations. The proposed validation framework provides a tool to mitigate risk when selecting AI solutions. Organizations should prioritize AI vendors providing high-evidence validation and public datasets, and implement governance frameworks based on the SURVAS system before deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: A systematic review of 102 surgical AI studies covering 2.8 million patients examined validation methodologies and clinical applications. Researchers developed the Surgical Validation Score classification system to standardize evidence assessment. Most AI applications targeted preoperative risk stratification and clinical decision support. Critical findings revealed only 45% of studies employed high-quality validation approaches and merely 14% released datasets publicly. The SURVAS framework enables clinicians to assess model reliability before clinical implementation, addressing significant gaps in standardized validation protocols and reproducibility.

papers.note: Four phase safety, efficacy, effectiveness and monitoring model, a clean structure for staging a clinical AI rollout.
papers.title: Clinical trials informed framework for real world clinical implementation and deployment of artificial intelligence applications
papers.explain_beginner: Healthcare organizations are deploying artificial intelligence tools but lack clear guidance on doing so safely. This paper proposes a four-step framework borrowed from how medical treatments are tested in clinical trials. Organizations should first verify the AI system works correctly, then confirm it produces the intended results, then compare it against existing methods, and finally monitor its performance over time. This structured approach helps ensure AI in healthcare is reliable and benefits patients fairly.
papers.explain_business: Organizations planning healthcare AI investments need a proven roadmap to reduce deployment risk and ensure adoption succeeds. This framework provides that roadmap by breaking implementation into four validated stages, similar to drug approval processes. Executives can use this structure to allocate resources appropriately, set realistic timelines, and demonstrate to stakeholders that deployments meet safety and effectiveness standards. Following this approach protects against costly failures and positions organizations to capture the full value of AI investments.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors present a four-phase implementation model for clinical AI deployment. Phase one validates safety, phase two demonstrates efficacy, phase three establishes effectiveness through comparison with existing standards, and phase four implements ongoing monitoring. This framework parallels established clinical trial methodology, providing implementers with a structured pathway from development to real-world use. The approach emphasizes institutional collaboration and seeking funding support to enable rigorous, systematic AI deployment that prioritizes patient outcomes and equitable access.

papers.note: Addresses the hard case of systems that keep learning after deployment, which fixed trial designs cannot cover.
papers.title: Rethinking clinical trials for medical AI with dynamic deployments of adaptive systems
papers.explain_beginner: Medical AI systems, especially those using large language models, keep learning and improving after they're released to hospitals. Traditional clinical trials test a frozen system once, then it goes live unchanged. This paper proposes a better approach where AI systems continue learning in real hospitals under careful monitoring. Doctors can track whether the system stays safe and effective as it adapts, catching problems quickly rather than discovering them months later.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying medical AI can now move beyond choosing between slow traditional approval or risky unmonitored deployment. Dynamic deployment enables companies to launch learning systems while maintaining regulatory compliance through continuous monitoring. This reduces time-to-market for evolving medical AI, supports faster improvement cycles, and provides documented evidence of safety and effectiveness in actual clinical use, ultimately enabling more sophisticated medical AI applications to reach patients sooner.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper presents dynamic deployment as a clinical trial framework designed for continuously-learning AI systems in medical settings. Unlike conventional trials that validate static models pre-deployment, this approach enables large language model-based medical AI to learn from real clinical interactions and new data post-deployment while maintaining concurrent monitoring and validation. The framework permits complex adaptive systems to operate in clinical environments with real-time safety oversight and performance assessment throughout their operational lifecycle.

papers.note: A working health system governance structure with committees, guiding principles and a value stream, not just principles.
papers.title: Governance of Clinical AI applications to facilitate safe and equitable deployment in a large health system

papers.note: Recent PRISMA review of AI in clinical risk management, covering incident reporting, falls and medication error.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: transforming patient safety with intelligent systems: A systematic review
papers.explain_beginner: Hospitals face serious problems from medical errors that harm patients and erode trust in healthcare. This research review examined how artificial intelligence could help prevent these mistakes. Scientists found that AI tools can successfully spot dangerous situations, predict medication errors, and identify patients at risk of falling or developing pressure wounds. However, putting these systems into actual hospitals remains difficult due to organizational and technical challenges that need solving before widespread adoption.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations exploring patient safety investments should recognize AI's validated capability in error prevention and incident detection. Practical applications exist for medication safety, fall prevention, and wound management. However, executives must account for significant implementation costs related to organizational change, staff training, and system integration challenges. Success requires partnerships with vendors willing to address regulatory standards and clinical workflow requirements. This technology represents a strategic opportunity, but requires phased implementation with clear metrics rather than immediate enterprise-wide deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: This PRISMA-compliant systematic review evaluated AI applications in clinical risk management across incident reporting, falls prevention, and medication safety. Researchers screened studies using Rayyan across multiple databases. Machine learning and natural language processing demonstrated effectiveness in adverse event detection, error prediction, risk stratification, and automated incident classification. Key findings revealed improved reporting accuracy and high-risk identification, though socio-technical barriers, implementation obstacles, and standardization gaps limit clinical integration. The authors recommend continued development with iterative refinement and regulatory alignment before scaling these systems in healthcare environments.

papers.note: Defines clinical hazards, constrains the action space, and retrains for safety without losing performance, a replicable method.
papers.title: Assuring the safety of AI-based clinical decision support systems: a case study of the AI Clinician for sepsis treatment
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested an AI system designed to recommend treatments for sepsis, a life-threatening infection. They identified four dangerous medical situations the AI should avoid, then checked whether the AI made safer recommendations than human doctors. The AI performed better in most cases. The team then adjusted how the AI learns to prioritize safety, and confirmed the improved version made safer choices without becoming less effective overall. This work shows how to carefully verify AI medical tools are trustworthy before using them in hospitals.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates a practical framework for safely deploying AI in clinical settings before regulatory approval. By systematically identifying medical risks and retraining the system to avoid them, the company can build confidence with hospitals and regulators. The approach preserves the AI's effectiveness while eliminating dangerous recommendations, reducing liability and approval timelines. This methodology is reproducible across different AI applications and clinical domains, providing a competitive advantage in developing trustworthy medical AI products that regulators will more readily approve for real-world deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: We conducted safety assurance on an AI Clinician reinforcement learning system for sepsis management. We defined four clinical hazards based on expert consensus and literature review, then identified unsafe scenarios to constrain the agent's action space. Testing against MIMIC-III data showed the AI recommended fewer hazardous decisions than clinicians in three of four scenarios. We modified the reward function to enforce safety constraints and retrained the model. The resulting agent demonstrated improved safety while maintaining predictive performance, establishing a replicable methodology for systematic safety assurance of autonomous clinical decision support systems.

papers.note: Nurses performed worse when the AI was misleading, so model accuracy alone does not make the joint system safe.
papers.title: Empirically derived evaluation requirements for responsible deployments of AI in safety-critical settings
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether artificial intelligence could help nurses spot medical emergencies faster. They found that while AI accuracy matters, it is not enough on its own. When the AI gave wrong explanations, nurses made worse decisions, even if the AI's answers were correct. The study shows that deploying AI in hospitals requires testing how humans and AI work together, not just checking if the AI works well by itself.
papers.explain_business: Organizations considering AI deployment in safety-critical environments like healthcare need assessment protocols beyond vendor accuracy claims. This research demonstrates that poor AI explanations actively harm decision quality despite correct recommendations, creating liability risks. Decision makers should require vendors to demonstrate human-AI team performance on diverse test cases, including scenarios where the AI performs poorly, before deployment approval or purchase decisions.
papers.explain_practitioner: This empirical study evaluated three augmentative AI systems for clinical decision support with 450 nursing students and 12 licensed nurses assessing 10 patient cases. Results demonstrated that nurse performance improved with accurate AI but degraded significantly when receiving misleading explanations, regardless of algorithmic correctness. The authors propose two evaluation requirements for safety-critical AI deployment: measure joint human-AI system performance empirically rather than AI performance alone, and test across cases generating varied AI quality levels to identify failure modes.
